title: Fleet commissioning, seatbelt scripts, and Terraform notes
content:
Purpose:
This note collects practical commissioning tasks and small 'seatbelt' scripts we run during on-prem k8s fleet bring-up. Goal is a set of idempotent checks and tiny helpers that reduce human error during initial provisioning and during upgrades. This is intentionally pragmatic — lean scripts and explicit checks, not a big orchestration rewrite.

Scope and assumptions:
- Target clusters: 3 control-plane nodes + N worker nodes (N varies per customer).
- Hardware: mixed Dell R650 + HPE ProLiant. Firmware baseline must be applied before commissioning (see firmware checklist link above).
- Network: management VLAN (PXE/ignition), data VLAN for pods, and an out-of-band management network (iDRAC/iLO).
- This doc focuses on baremetal and vSphere-provisioned baremetal-equivalents (VM control plane with dedicated worker racks).
- We assume Terraform for infra binding (IPAM, DNS records, VLAN attachments) and Ansible for node-level config; scripts live in ops-scripts repo.

Why 'seatbelt' scripts?
- Long playbooks are hard to iterate in the field. Small, focused scripts verifying one invariant (eg. 'verify-kv-cache-paths', 'check-ksm-available-memory') are easy to run, re-run, and combine.
- They serve as midway automation: quick safeguards between manual ops and full automation.

High-level commissioning flow (recommended):
1) Inventory import: pull BMC/IPMI inventory into terraform-data (CSV -> terraform var).
2) PXE & ignition validation: confirm TFTP/HTTP server reachability from each BMC + node.
3) Node-level seatbelts (run in parallel):
   - seatbelt-bmc-health.sh: verifies BMC credentials, reachable, firmware level.
   - seatbelt-disk-metadata.sh: checks disk serials, SMART baseline, RAID metadata mismatch.
   - seatbelt-nvme-paths.sh: ensures NVMe namespaces exposed and stable across reboots.
   - seatbelt-rtc-sync.sh: validate RTC and timezone; mismatch can break cert rotation.
4) Network sanity: ipmi-to-hostpath test, switch port VLAN tagging check, MTU test across pod network.
5) Terraform apply: create DNS entries, IP allocations, loadbalancer objects.
6) Bootstrap control plane: execute immutable control-plane init (kubeadm/metal3/ignition flow) with pre-flight seatbelts.
7) Join workers and run post-join checks: kubelet registration, taints, CNI health.
8) Canary deploy a small service and run throughput/latency quick checks.

Idempotent Terraform module notes (practical observations):
- Keep modules small: ipam, dns, vlan-attachment, bootserver-binding. Each module should expose a stable resource id that is safe to reapply even if other modules change.
- Avoid modules that both create and mutate DHCP options dynamically — DHCP leases are ephemeral and cause drift problems. Instead: terraform manages static DHCP ranges and a small labeling key used by provisioning to pick a subnet.
- Use 'lifecycle ignore_changes' sparingly for provider-managed fields that will be mutated by downstream provisioning (eg. vm.power_state). Document every ignore change with an inline comment in the module.
- Export a 'provisioning-token' secret from the infra module (short TTL) that ignition uses for the first-stage bootstrap. Rotate this token on any re-run where control plane manifests have changed.

Seatbelt script examples (conceptual snippets):
- seatbelt-bmc-health.sh:
  #!/bin/bash
  set -euo pipefail
  for host in $(cat hosts.txt); do
    ipmihealth=$(ipmitool -I lanplus -H $host -U $BMC_USER -P $BMC_PASS sdr elist | grep -i voltage || true)
    if [[ -z "$ipmihealth" ]]; then echo "WARN $host: no voltage reading"; fi
  done

- seatbelt-kube-object-check.py (python): connect to cluster, assert nodes==expected, check kubelet versions all in supported range.

Testing and verification checklist (quick run):
- control-plane kube-apiserver logs for restart loops (past 5 minutes)
- etcd member list has quorum and acceptable latency (etcdctl endpoint status)
- coredns forwarding success and 200s for pod -> external DNS
- sample load test: 5 pods calling a simple echo service, 95th percentile latency < 200ms on 10k token-equivalent workload (approx).

Upgrade and rollback heuristics (operational guidance):
- Always run seatbelts pre-upgrade and record outputs in a 'provisioning-artifact' directory (timestamped). These artifacts are the primary input for rollbacks.
- Control plane upgrades: one control-plane node at a time, run seatbelts + kubelet-version-check after rejoin. Pause rollouts on any certificate expiry warnings.
- Worker upgrades: cordon -> drain -> apply image/OS upgrade -> uncordon. After each worker rejoin, run quick e2e smoke (pod scheduling & KV-cache warm).
- Rollback strategy: if control-plane fails to reach quorum after step N, revert to previous etcd snapshot from t0 (taken immediately prior to upgrade). Our ops-scripts provide etcd snapshot helpers (etcd-snapshot-rotate.sh).

Operational anti-patterns we've seen:
- Running terraform apply while provisioning is mid-flight (leads to IP collisions). Stale DHCP state + terraform drift causes repeated reboots. Fix: enforce a staging lock via a small state file in S3/GCS with a TTL.
- Over-reliance on a single monolithic playbook that tries to do everything; when it fails, it's hard to recover. Prefer small verified steps.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we add a non-root seatbelt runner that runs from the admin jumpbox and posts results to a central 'provisioning-audit' endpoint? (ask SRE infra team).
- Should we formalize a minimal JSON schema for seatbelt outputs so the console can ingest them for per-deployment SLOs? (proto draft in ops-scripts repo).
- Confirm recommended etcd snapshot cadence for clusters with >1000 pods. Current heuristics: every 10 minutes during upgrades, hourly otherwise. Need more data.

Notes to self / field tips:
- Always check switch optics — port mismatches with SFPs are silent killers during PXE.
- On vSphere-based private deployments, control plane VMs should use paravirtual SCSI for disk stability; note this in terraform variables for the customer.
- Keep a small set of golden ignition/user-data templates per SKU; name them with sku+boot-env-version for traceability.

Appendix: quick command cheatsheet
- Verify etcd: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=$EP endpoint status
- List nodes and versions: kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,VER:.status.nodeInfo.kubeletVersion
- Snapshot etcd: etcdctl snapshot save /artifacts/snap-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).db

If this doc looks useful, next step is to extract the seatbelt scripts from ops-scripts into a dedicated 'provisioning-seatbelts' dir and add a basic CI lint that asserts scripts exit 0 on a mock inventory.
